title: Module 2: Lexical Scope, Hoisting & Variable Declarations (All Chapters)
description: Comprehensive module-level assessment covering all chapters of Module 2: Lexical Scope, Hoisting & Variable Declarations.

cards.concept: Scope Hierarchy & Global Context: Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
cards.question: What causes a `ReferenceError` when accessing a `let` or `const` identifier before its syntactic declaration?

options.text: The identifier is never hoisted during compile phase.
The identifier is hoisted into the declarative environment record, but remains uninitialized in the TDZ until evaluated.
The identifier is assigned `undefined` which prohibits read access.
Block scopes delete uninitialized identifiers at runtime.

cards.explanation: let and const declarations are hoisted to the top of their enclosing block, but remain in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). Accessing them before initialization throws ReferenceError.
cards.codeSnippet:
// console.log(val); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'val' before initialization
let val = 42;
cards.pitfall: Using typeof on a TDZ variable does not safely return 'undefined'; it throws ReferenceError unlike genuinely undeclared variables.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §14.3.1 / You Don't Know JS: Scope & Closures

cards.concept: Scope Hierarchy & Global Context: Function Declaration vs Expression Hoisting
cards.question: Why can a function declaration be invoked before its syntactic definition, while a `var` or `const` function expression cannot?

options.text: Function declarations are compiled into WebAssembly at startup.
Function declarations are hoisted with their complete function bodies during environment record instantiation.
Function expressions run in separate isolates.
Strict mode forbids invoking function declarations before declaration.

cards.explanation: Function declarations have both identifier and function value initialized during compile/instantiation phase, whereas function expressions assign the value only when statement execution occurs.
cards.pitfall: Calling a var function expression before definition results in TypeError (undefined is not a function), whereas let/const results in ReferenceError.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §15.2 / MDN Web Docs: Hoisting
